stories.title: UP flood situation: 3 killed, over 16K evacuated from 23 affected districts
stories.summary: As many as 16,784 people have been evacuated to safety so far, with 3,042 of them rescued on Wednesday, as flood conditions persisted in parts of Uttar Pradesh, with 23 districts currently affected out of 35 districts impacted so far, officials said. Three people have died in rain-related incidents -- 18-month-old Priyansh in Pratapgarh and Shera, 32, and Suresh, 55, in Amroha's Gajraula. The government said 1,499 boats and motorboats have been deployed for relief and rescue operations, while 1,067 medical teams have been pressed into service. The affected districts are Ayodhya, Azamgarh, Ballia, Barabanki, Badaun, Chandauli, Farrukhabad, Ghazipur, Gorakhpur, Hardoi, Kasganj, Lakhimpur Kheri, Mirzapur, Moradabad, Pilibhit, Prayagraj, Raebareli, Sant Kabir Nagar, Shahjahanpur, Sitapur, Sonbhadra, Unnao and Varanasi, it said in the evening. The government has established 1,311 flood shelters, of which 201 are currently operational. Relief agencies have also provided assistance in 442

stories.headline: MP Aga Ruhullah urges Budgam administration to reopen Yousmarg tourist resort
stories.title: MP Aga Ruhullah urges Budgam administration to reopen Yousmarg tourist resort
stories.summary: Srinagar MP Aga Syed Ruhullah Mehdi has urged the Budgam district administration to immediately reopen the tourist resort Yousmarg, citing severe economic distress faced by locals dependent on tourism for their survival. In a communication to the Deputy Commissioner of Budgam accessed by news agency KNS, the Lok Sabha member said a delegation of residents from Yousmarg had recently met him and expressed "serious concern" over the continued restrictions, especially when other tourist hotspots across the Union Territory are functioning normally. "The local residents expressed serious concern that when other major tourist destinations in Jammu & Kashmir are open and receiving visitors, Yousmarg should also be considered for reopening, subject to all necessary safety and administrative protocols," the MP said in his letter. Describing tourism as the "primary source of livelihood" for the area, MP Mehdi pointed out that pony operators, horse riders, hoteliers, shopkeepers, transporters and tour guides have been the worst hit by the prolonged curbs, with many families struggling to make ends meet. "In view of the above, I request your good office to kindly examine the matter on priority and take appropriate steps for reopening Yousmarg for tourists, if there are no prevailing security or administrative constraints," he wrote. He further appealed to the administration to give "due consideration" to the livelihood concerns of the local population while taking any decision. Yousmarg a tourist destination in central Kashmir's Budgam district remained largely inaccessible to tourists since security measures were tightened following the 2025 Pahalgam terror attack. Although authorities had allowed limited movement earlier this year, the flow of visitors has remained negligible, dealing a crippling blow to the local economy. Notably, Local stakeholders have repeatedly demanded the removal of restrictions, warning that the continued shutdown could push many families into irreversible financial ruin.

stories.headline: Public protest reflects failure to address grievances by NC Govt: LOP
stories.title: Public protest reflects failure to address grievances by NC Govt: LOP
stories.summary: Srinagar, Sep 2: Leader of Opposition (LOP) and senior Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leader Sunil Sharma on Wednesday launched a sharp attack on Chief Minister Omar Abdullah-led government, saying the large public participation in the BJP’s protest in Srinagar reflected growing discontent over what he termed the administration’s failure to address people’s concerns. “Thousands of people took to the streets against CM Omar-led government. This is a reflection of its failure, where people are worried and their problems remain unresolved,” Sharma said. He alleged that the government had failed the youth and “snatched away” their rights, particularly on issues concerning employment and recruitment. “That is why these people have come out on the streets,” he said. Sharma said the government’s alleged failures were now visible on the streets, claiming that the issues being raised by protesters were directly linked to the everyday concerns of the people. The BJP protest, led by J&K unit president and Rajya Sabha MP Sat Sharma and LOP Sunil Sharma, began at Ghanta Ghar in Lal Chowk, with party workers marching towards the civil secretariat. Protesters raised slogans against the government over unemployment, electricity tariffs, alleged corruption, recruitment issues, and other governance-related concerns. The BJP also highlighted the recent 6.83 percent electricity tariff hike, alleged backdoor appointments, and outsourcing of government jobs, besides the reported failure to implement the promise of 200 units of free electricity. Police and paramilitary personnel intercepted the march near Hari Singh High Street, short of the civil secretariat, amid heightened security arrangements in central Srinagar. Roads around Lal Chowk were also closed to vehicular movement as security forces were deployed at several strategic points. Addressing party workers, Sharma said the BJP protest was focused on four major issues — alleged irregularities in government recruitment, delay in holding local body and panchayat elections, corruption, and the increase in electricity tariffs. He accused the government of failing to adequately address issues related to electricity, water, roads, unemployment, and other basic concerns while continuing to focus its political narrative on restoration of statehood. Sharma also challenged CM Omar to resign from his Ganderbal Assembly seat and seek a fresh mandate from the people on the issue of statehood. “If you have any self-respect left, fight an election on it. Only then will we acknowledge it as your issue,” he said.

stories.headline: Face-off: NC, BJP hold protests over statehood, governance in J&K
stories.title: Face-off: NC, BJP hold protests over statehood, governance in J&K
stories.summary: Srinagar, Sep 2: Jammu and Kashmir witnessed a sharp political face-off on Wednesday as the ruling National Conference (NC) and opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) staged rival protests in Srinagar, turning the streets into a political battleground over restoration of statehood, governance and promises made to the people. The NC protested against the BJP-led central government over the delay in restoring statehood to J&K, while the BJP demonstrated against the Chief Minister Omar Abdullah-led government, accusing it of failing to deliver on electoral commitments relating to jobs, corruption, local body elections, and power tariffs. Both parties attempted to march towards their respective targets but were stopped by police. The developments marked one of the most prominent instances of rival political mobilisation in J&K since the August 2019 constitutional changes, with both the ruling party and the principal opposition choosing street protests to put their political opponents under pressure. The NC had announced a march towards the BJP headquarters in Jawahar Nagar, where it planned to stage a gherao to demand restoration of statehood. Senior party leaders, including Health and Education Minister Sakina Itoo and MLAs Tanvir Sadiq, Salman Sagar, Ahsan Pardesi, Shamima Firdous, Nazir Gurezi, Javid Baig, and Abdul Majeed Larmi, assembled near the Gindun Sports Complex in Rajbagh. The protesters raised slogans demanding restoration of statehood and the constitutional guarantees withdrawn following the August 5, 2019 decisions. Police and security personnel erected barricades near the Rajbagh police station and stopped the NC march from proceeding towards Jawahar Nagar. Some protesters were subsequently detained amid a confrontation with security forces. The NC accused the administration of preventing people from joining the demonstration and alleged that some of its elected representatives were mishandled. “The JKNC's peaceful protest was stopped from moving forward. People were prevented from joining, and elected representatives were mishandled. Yet, when the BJP held a protest outside the civil secretariat, it was allowed to proceed. What a shame!” the party said on X. NC chief spokesman and MLA Zadibal Tanvir Sadiq said the Centre had delayed its commitment to restore statehood for too long. “Where is statehood? It has been two years since the elections. The time has come to fulfil the promise made to us,” he said. MLA Hazratbal Salman Sagar, who participated in the NC mobilisation, also hit out at the BJP over its counter-protest and defended the NC's decision to take the issue to the streets. Sagar questioned the BJP's position on statehood, arguing that the opposition party could not criticise the NC for raising an issue on which the BJP itself had made a commitment to the people of J&K. He maintained that the NC would continue to press for restoration of statehood and would not allow the issue to be pushed into the background. The NC leadership said it had waited for two years following the Assembly elections for the Centre to act on its commitment. Restoration of full statehood has remained one of CM Omar and the NC's principal political demands. The party also raised the issue of reservation rationalisation, arguing that the matter had significant implications for the future of J&K's youth. CM's Adviser Nasir Aslam Wani said the government had been waiting for the Centre to fulfil commitments made to the people. “For two years, we have been sitting patiently and waiting with the hope that the promises made to us would be fulfilled. People had expected statehood to be restored after the elections, but no concrete discussion had taken place on the issue,” Wani said. While the NC targeted the Centre, the BJP simultaneously took aim at the elected government in Srinagar. The BJP took its political battle to the streets of Srinagar on Wednesday, holding protests that prompted heavy security deployment and police intervention to keep them apart. Hundreds of BJP workers, led by J&K unit president and Rajya Sabha MP Sat Sharma and Leader of Opposition (LOP) Sunil Sharma, gathered at the Ghanta Ghar in Lal Chowk and marched towards the civil secretariat, the seat of the J&K government, with the intention of gheraoing it. The protesters raised slogans against the CM Omar-led government, accusing it of failing to address unemployment, power supply, corruption, and other public grievances nearly two years after the 2024 assembly polls. Carrying placards, BJP workers highlighted the recent 6.83 percent electricity tariff hike, alleged backdoor appointments, outsourcing of government jobs, and the government’s unfulfilled promise of providing 200 units of free electricity. Protesters also burnt an effigy of CM Omar. Police stopped the BJP march near the Hari Singh High Street-Jahangir Chowk area after deploying barricades. Protesters attempted to move forward but were prevented from reaching the civil secretariat. A small group of protesters, however, reportedly managed to reach the civil secretariat complex. Roads around Lal Chowk were sealed to vehicular traffic, while large contingents of security forces were deployed at key locations to prevent any confrontation between rival political groups. Addressing the protesters, Sunil Sharma said the BJP demonstration was centred on four issues — alleged sale of government jobs instead of transparent recruitment, delay in holding local body and panchayat elections, alleged corruption, and the increase in electricity tariffs. He accused the government of failing to address issues concerning electricity, water, roads, and unemployment while focusing its political campaign primarily on restoration of statehood. He accused the government of failing to fulfil its electoral commitments and alleged that jobs were being “sold” rather than being filled through a fair and transparent recruitment process. The BJP leader also questioned the NC's emphasis on statehood, arguing that the elected government should focus on governance and issues affecting ordinary people. Taking a swipe at CM Omar, Sharma asked whether voters had elected the CM to “live like a prince and go skiing in Gulmarg and Pahalgam”. He challenged CM Omar to resign from his Ganderbal Assembly seat and seek a fresh mandate specifically on the statehood issue. “If you have any self-respect left, fight an election on statehood,” Sharma said. He argued that if CM Omar secured a fresh mandate on statehood, the BJP would accept that the issue was genuinely the NC's political agenda. Otherwise, he said, the party should stop using the issue to mislead the public. Sharma also said statehood was not an issue that could be claimed exclusively by the NC, pointing out that the BJP too had promised to restore statehood to J&K at an appropriate time. Sharma said the large public participation in the protest reflected what he described as the administration’s failure to resolve people’s grievances. “Thousands of people have taken to the streets against the CM Omar-led government. This is a reflection of its failure, where people are worried and their problems remain unresolved,” he said. Sharma alleged that the government had “snatched away” the rights of the youth and failed to fulfil its promises. “The government that did injustice to the youth here, took away their rights. That is why these people have come out on the streets. The government’s failure is visible on the streets today,” he said. J&K BJP president and Rajya Sabha member Sat Sharma described the demonstration as a warning to the CM Omar-led government, saying it should either live up to people's expectations or resign. He also claimed that the turnout demonstrated a change in Srinagar’s political atmosphere. The rival protests subsequently triggered a political controversy over the administration's handling of demonstrations. The NC accused the authorities of giving greater freedom to the BJP while restricting its own protest. “A tale of two protests. One, facilitated and allowed freely. The other, roughed up and restricted. Same administration, different attitude,” the party said on X. PDP President Mehbooba Mufti also questioned the manner in which the protests were handled, accusing the administration of applying different standards to political parties. “The same police that won't allow PDP to step outside its office to hold a peaceful protest on public issues have facilitated both the BJP and the NC to protest against each other,” Mufti said. She questioned who authorised what she described as selective restrictions and why the law was allegedly being applied differently to different political parties. The political confrontation was not confined to Srinagar. In Jammu, dozens of NC workers led by Jammu provincial president Rattan Lal Gupta assembled at the Trikuta Nagar market and attempted to march towards the BJP headquarters. Police stopped the march and erected barricades to block the protesters. When some workers attempted to cross the barricades, they were detained. Wednesday’s developments marked one of the most visible political confrontations between the NC government and the BJP on the streets of Srinagar in recent years, reflecting growing tensions over governance, employment, and the unresolved issue of statehood.

stories.headline: NC concedes governance Failure, reacts frantically to massive BJP protest
stories.title: NC concedes governance Failure, reacts frantically to massive BJP protest
stories.summary: The National Conference appears to have been rattled by the massive “Secretariat Chalo” protest organised by the BJP against the Omar Abdullah government. In what looked more like a hurried counter-response than a serious political mobilisation, the NC announced and staged a protest near the BJP offices in Srinagar and Jammu. The contrast could hardly have been more striking: a principal opposition party marching towards the seat of government to raise public issues, and a ruling party responding with what appeared to be a political photo-op. What a fall from political grace. As the principal opposition party in Jammu Kashmir, the BJP has consistently raised issues concerning ordinary citizens, both inside the Assembly and on the streets. The Secretariat Gherao at the Civil Secretariat in Srinagar was part of a wider campaign against alleged backdoor appointments, outsourcing of employment, electricity tariff increases and, most importantly, the National Conference government's alleged U-turns on promises made before and during the 2024 Assembly elections. The recent electricity tariff hike may have provided the immediate trigger, but the NC government faces a problem much larger than the 6.83 per cent increase approved by the Joint Electricity Regulatory Commission. It faces a credibility deficit. There may be an economic explanation for increasing electricity tariffs. Power-sector finances, transmission and distribution losses, revenue recovery and rising costs are genuine issues that any responsible government must address. But the NC government's political defence of the hike raises a far more uncomfortable question: What happens to electoral promises once the party that made them comes to power? In its 2024 Assembly election manifesto, the National Conference made a specific commitment to provide 200 units of free electricity. The promise was presented without any obvious qualification. The party also promised a one-time settlement of pending electricity-bill arrears in rural and urban areas and stated that it would explore ways to provide relief in power tariffs to promote industrial growth and sustainability. This was not an obscure promise buried in the manifesto. It was publicly projected by Omar Abdullah as one of the party's important electoral guarantees. Yet nearly two years after the election, the promised universal 200 units of free electricity remain nowhere in sight. Instead, consumers are confronted with higher tariffs. The Joint Electricity Regulatory Commission has approved an average 6.83 per cent tariff increase from September 1, 2026, triggering public criticism and political protests. Chief Minister Omar Abdullah has defended the decision as a “compulsion” and has argued that his government never promised that electricity tariffs would remain frozen. That argument may be technically defensible, but politically it misses the point. The voter did not ask for a legal interpretation of the word “free”. The voter heard a simple electoral promise: 200 units of electricity free of cost. The issue, therefore, is not whether electricity tariffs can ever increase. Responsible governments may sometimes have no alternative. The real question is why a party that promised relief from the electricity burden has presided over a tariff increase before delivering the principal relief it promised. article_sentences: New Delhi: The Supreme Court on Wednesday allowed Oil India Limited (OIL) to withdraw its interlocutory application challenging the Centre's refusal to approve its Extended Reach Drilling (ERD) project for extracting hydrocarbons beneath Assam's Dibru-Saikhowa National Park, with liberty to file a fresh petition.
A bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana passed the order after senior advocate Rakesh Dwivedi, appearing for OIL, sought urgent hearing of the matter.
Dwivedi said the project was crucial to the country's energy requirements and involved drilling from outside the national park to reach hydrocarbon reserves located 3,500-4,000 metres underground.
He argued that ERD was not conventional mining and that the drilling infrastructure would remain outside the protected area.
OIL has challenged the Forest Advisory Committee's decision and the Environment Ministry's refusal to approve diversion of 0.069 hectares of forest land for the project.

The company contended that the authorities wrongly relied on the Supreme Court's 2023 order restricting mining in and around protected areas, and has also cited earlier orders permitting sub-surface hydrocarbon extraction beneath the park using ERD technology.

The company has also relied on earlier orders of the top court in 2017, when it was permitted, subject to conditions and safeguards, to extract hydrocarbons beneath the national park using ERD technology.

It said the Standing Committee of the National Board for Wildlife had recommended the proposal and that the top court subsequently allowed sub-surface hydrocarbon extraction, subject to compliance with environmental and wildlife protection conditions.
It sought to set aside the order of August 02, 2024 passed by the MoEFCC and also the minutes of the meeting of the Forest Advisory Committee of the MoEFCC on July 4, 2024.

stories.headline: Can solar power finally break J&K’s electricity crisis cycle?
stories.title: Can solar power finally break J&K’s electricity crisis cycle?
stories.summary: Srinagar, Sep 2: Jammu and Kashmir’s recurring electricity crisis may have a partial solution in three developments already taking shape — rooftop solar, smart metering and the newly introduced Time-of-Day (ToD) tariff. Taken together, these measures could reduce dependence on costly grid power, flatten peak demand and, over time, help contain electricity costs. The government has already begun with its own buildings. A major rooftop solarisation programme covering thousands of government establishments is under implementation, with official plans running into hundreds of megawatts. The programme provides for net metering and bidirectional smart meters, allowing government buildings to consume their own solar generation and feed surplus electricity into the grid. JERC’s new ToD tariff can complement this effort. Consumers with sanctioned load above 10 kW and compatible metering are eligible for a 20 percent rebate during the 9 am-5 pm solar period, while specified peak-hour consumption attracts a surcharge. Government offices, colleges, universities and other institutions largely function during these daytime hours. They can therefore benefit from the rebate even before their rooftop systems are fully installed. Once solarised, their dependence on grid electricity during the day could fall further. This should now become an accountability issue for the Finance and Power Departments. Government establishments should identify every flexible load that can be shifted towards solar hours. Pumping stations, lift and irrigation schemes, workshops, and similar operations should be examined individually. Where storage or operational flexibility permits, there is little logic in running heavy loads during the evening peak when they could instead be operated during periods of abundant solar generation. The benefit would extend beyond government electricity bills. Every flexible load shifted away from the evening peak releases grid capacity precisely when households need electricity most for heating, cooking and lighting. Better demand management could therefore help reduce the pressure that contributes to winter curtailments. Industry should be the next major participant. The existing J&K Industrial Policy provides substantial support for DG sets. The policy is now under revision, and the government has emphasised green energy and reducing industry’s carbon footprint during stakeholder consultations. If the revised policy ultimately replaces or redirects conventional DG-set support towards rooftop solar, it would represent a logical transition — from subsidising diesel-based backup to supporting clean captive generation. The new framework should make such a transition meaningful enough to encourage existing industries to participate as well. The combination with ToD makes the case particularly relevant for Kashmir’s single-shift industries. A unit operating predominantly between 9 am and 5 pm can benefit from the existing daytime tariff rebate, while rooftop solar can meet a significant share of its electricity requirement during the same period. JAKEDA has also identified grid-connected rooftop solar across commercial and industrial sectors as a means of substantially reducing electricity drawn from the utility grid. But the biggest opportunity lies with households. The sheer number of domestic consumers means that even modest changes in household generation and consumption patterns could have a significant system-wide impact. J&K already has a substantial household rooftop-solar programme under way. Official information placed before Parliament showed 39,160 rooftop installations completed against 85,908 applications as of July 28, 2026. During the preceding five years, Rs 278.55 crore in central assistance had been released to J&K under rooftop-solar programmes. The gap between applications and completed installations, however, shows the scale of the unfinished task. Domestic solarisation now needs to be pursued with considerably greater urgency. There is another policy gap. Ordinary households are currently outside the JERC ToD provision because it applies to consumers above 10 kW. That leaves the largest consumer base without the very incentive that could encourage changes in consumption behaviour. As smart metering expands, the government could consider approaching JERC for a dedicated domestic ToD incentive for smart-metered consumers. Such a mechanism need not initially impose a peak-hour surcharge. A meaningful daytime rebate alone could encourage households to shift flexible consumption — washing, ironing, water heating, pumping and other electricity-intensive activities - towards solar hours. Nor should the policy necessarily wait until every household in J&K has a smart meter. The incentive could progressively be extended wherever compatible metering, billing and regulatory systems permit. The sequence is therefore straightforward. government can lead by solarising its buildings and shifting flexible loads into daylight hours. Industry and commerce can follow through rooftop solar and ToD incentives. Households can be brought into the solar programme at greater speed and gradually offered incentives to consume more electricity during the day. For decades, J&K’s electricity debate has focused primarily on one question: how much more power can the system generate or purchase? The next phase should ask two additional questions: how much electricity can be generated where it is consumed, and when should the remaining grid power be consumed? Solarise the roofs. Incentivise daytime consumption. Reduce the evening peak. If rooftop solar, smart metering and ToD tariffs are pursued as parts of one integrated demand-management strategy rather than as disconnected programmes, J&K may finally begin addressing not only its power deficit, but the structural pattern that keeps producing an electricity crisis.

stories.headline: Auqib Nabi begins County stint with Surrey
stories.title: Auqib Nabi begins County stint with Surrey
stories.summary: Jammu and Kashmir pacer Auqib Nabi has joined Surrey for a three-match stint in the County Championship, with the move providing the promising seamer an opportunity to gain experience of English conditions ahead of India’s tour of New Zealand later this year. Nabi, who recently received his maiden India call-up as a replacement for injured Jasprit Bumrah for the two-Test series against Sri Lanka, has travelled to the United Kingdom and is set to make his Surrey debut against Yorkshire at The Oval on Wednesday. The 29-year-old will also be available for Surrey’s next two matches against Sussex in Hove from September 8-11 and Glamorgan at The Oval from September 15-18. The county side had been looking to strengthen its bowling attack, particularly with a swing bowler, and Nabi’s ability to move the ball is expected to be useful in the English conditions. The stint could also prove significant for Nabi’s international ambitions. Nabi has emerged as one of the most prolific uncapped fast bowlers in Indian domestic cricket. Representing Jammu and Kashmir, he was the leading wicket-taker in the 2025-26 Ranji Trophy, taking 60 wickets at an average of just over 12.5. His campaign included a five-wicket haul in the Ranji Trophy final, helping J&K clinch their maiden title, while he also claimed nine wickets in the semi-final. He has taken more than 100 wickets across the last two Ranji Trophy seasons and also grabbed headlines in the 2025 Duleep Trophy when he took four wickets in four balls for North Zone. His performances earned him an IPL contract with Delhi Capitals, for whom he played five matches during the 2026 season. Nabi is expected to return to India in time for the India A series against Australia A, beginning September 22 in Puducherry. “It’s an honour to join Surrey, one of the best clubs in England,” Nabi said.

stories.headline: Beyond the Ballot
stories.title: Beyond the Ballot
stories.summary: South Asia’s political landscape presents one of the most compelling narratives in contemporary democratic governance. Historically, the subcontinent stood at the forefront of female executive leadership, producing Sri Lanka’s Sirimavo Bandaranaike—the world’s first female prime minister in 1960 – alongside iconic heads of government including Indira Gandhi, Benazir Bhutto, Sheikh Hasina, and Khaleda Zia. Today, as regional democracies actively strive toward the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 5 (SDG-5) for gender equality, a profound democratic transition is unfolding from the grassroots upward. This evolving landscape demonstrates that women are decisively moving beyond passive voting toward becoming central architects of governance, even as key institutional and socio-cultural barriers remain to be addressed. The foundation of this democratic expansion was laid through India’s landmark 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments in 1993, which mandated a minimum 33.3% reservation for women across rural Panchayati Raj Institutions and urban local bodies. Over the subsequent decades, more than twenty Indian states – including Bihar, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, and West Bengal – progressively elevated this threshold to a 50% reservation. Today, nearly 1.4 million women hold elected office in Panchayats across India. Ground-breaking empirical research by Nobel laureate Esther Duflo and Raghabendra Chattopadhyay confirms that female local leaders systematically steer public spending toward vital community priorities, particularly clean drinking water, sanitation, fuel access, and rural road connectivity. Moreover, continuous exposure to female leadership has actively dismantled entrenched societal stereotypes, while significantly elevating the educational and professional aspirations of adolescent girls in rural communities. At the ballot box, female engagement has shattered historic records. In India’s 2024 general elections, the traditional gender turnout gap was inverted, with female voter turnout reaching an unprecedented 65.8%, marginally surpassing male turnout at 65.6%. In states such as West Bengal, female turnout reached 83.33%. Women have emerged as an autonomous, decisive voting constituency, prompting state governments to introduce programmatic welfare initiatives, including direct benefit transfers, educational stipends, and subsidized cooking gas. Complementing this electoral mobilization, India’s enactment of the historic Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam (Women’s Reservation Act) – mandating 33% representation in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies—marks a transformative institutional step toward scaling grassroots democratic representation into national parliamentary chambers. Across the wider South Asian neighbourhood, positive milestones coexist with valuable institutional lessons. Crucially, empirical research by PRS Legislative Research robustly refutes the traditional myth regarding female “winnability”. In contested general elections, female candidates achieve win rates equivalent to or exceeding those of their male counterparts, while demonstrating identical diligence in parliamentary attendance and debate. At the local level, newly elected representatives frequently encounter administrative and resource deficits. A large number of female Panchayat members receive limited formal training in budgetary allocation and bureaucratic procedures, while roughly half of rural administrative units lack adequate office facilities and digital connectivity. In the absence of institutional capacity-building, female leaders can face administrative sidelining or the challenge of proxy governance, wherein male relatives attempt to mediate council decisions. Similarly, in systems relying on indirect party-list quotas, such as in Bangladesh & Pakistan, female legislators often lack independent popular constituencies, leaving their legislative autonomy constrained by party hierarchies. Furthermore, the rising financial demands of electoral campaigning and the emergence of Violence Against Women in Politics (VAWP) remain serious deterrents. UN Women reports that 81.8% of surveyed female parliamentarians in the Asia-Pacific region experienced psychological harassment, while 44.4% faced explicit physical threats. In the digital sphere, cyber-VAWP—ranging from coordinated smear campaigns to weaponized artificial intelligence deepfakes – poses an escalating threat to female public figures. Bridging the gap between electoral participation and substantive empowerment requires concerted structural support. Strengthening internal democracy and campaign financing within political parties, enforcing strict legal protections against physical and digital harassment, and institutionalising continuous governance academies for local representatives are essential steps forward. By reinforcing these institutional foundations, South Asia can harness its surging female electorate to foster enduring democratic leadership and fully achieve the promise of SDG-5. These are excerpts from a paper presented on 18 August 2026 at a National Conference on “Gender Equality in the 21st Century: Perspectives and Pathways to SDG-5” held at Govt. Degree College for Women, M.A. Road Srinagar.

stories.headline: Agriculture sector provides 70% of livelihoods, contributes 18% to J&K GDP: Government
stories.title: Agriculture sector provides 70% of livelihoods, contributes 18% to J&K GDP: Government
stories.summary: Srinagar, Sep 2: Agriculture and allied activities provide around 70 per cent of livelihoods in Jammu and Kashmir and contribute about 18 per cent to the Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP), the official figures have revealed. As per the government statistics highlighting the agriculture sector’s progress between 2019-20 and 2025-26, the government has listed a series of achievements in the agriculture and allied sectors, including a more than two-fold increase in cold storage capacity, expansion of crop insurance, growth in milk and fish production and increased horticulture exports. As per the figures, cold storage capacity in J&K increased from 1.39 lakh metric tonnes to 2.97 lakh MT from 2019-20 to 2025-26. Under the PM Kisan Samman Nidhi scheme, Rs 4,383.61 crore has been disbursed to 9,16,587 lakh farmers, the document states. The government figures presented before the recently convened meeting with Niti Aayog members, the government said two Horticulture Centres of excellence and one Agriculture Centre of Excellence have been established, while 13 others are under execution. “The Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana has also been extended to all 20 districts,” the official document reads. The government claimed that the Kisan Credit Card scheme has 11.44 lakh active cards, with Rs 10,964 crore in loans sanctioned. “Milk processing capacity increased seven-fold, from 35,000 litres to 2.50 lakh litres per day, while fish production rose by 40 per cent from 21,000 MT to 31,700 MT,” the official document reads. As per the official statistics, seven agricultural products have received Geographical Indication (GI) tags, with 20 more products under process. “The National Agriculture Market has linked 17 mandis and registered 2,750 traders since 2019,” the official document reads. The government claimed that Horticulture exports also increased from 11.87 lakh MT in 2020-21 to 13.86 lakh MT in 2025-26. In the meeting, the government also highlighted progress under the Holistic Agriculture Development Programme (HADP), including the establishment of 1.46 lakh units and generation of 4 crore person-days of employment. “Under area expansion initiatives, 12,764 hectares have been brought under crops including Mushqbudji rice, red rice, chilli, hill garlic and vegetables,” the official document reads. The government informed the Niti Aayog team that 2.88 lakh farmers have been skilled through the DAKSH KISAN initiative. The document reads that mushroom production increased from 2,100 MT in 2021-22 to 3,765 MT, while honey production rose from 2,200 MT to 3,900 MT. The seed replacement rate has increased from 12 per cent to 20 per cent, while 1,150 saffron and 890 other nurseries have been registered. As per the official statistics, a total of 1,807 KissanKhidmatGhars have been established, with 9.41 lakh farmers registered and 5.2 lakh farms geo-tagged and on boarded. The HADP progress also includes the establishment of 481 Hi-Tech Poly Greenhouses covering 2.26 lakh square metres and 966 low-cost poly greenhouses covering 2.18 lakh square metres. As per the official data, under the Yellow Revolution, the area under oilseed cultivation has expanded from 1.40 lakh hectares. The document also outlines the Competitiveness Improvement of Agriculture and Allied Project (JK-CIP), a $217 million (approximately Rs 1,800 crore) project focused on improving the climate and market ecosystem across 90 blocks. The project targets marginal communities and women and is expected to benefit around three lakh households, or approximately 15 lakh people. “Its components include climate-smart and market-led production, development support for the agri-business ecosystem, and support to vulnerable communities and project management,” the document reads. The expected outcomes after seven years include scaling up collectivisation, strengthening and establishing Farmer Producer Organisations, supporting business-led enterprises, market support and brand development, assistance to startups and benefits to three lakh households. The government claimed that under JK-CIP, 65,123 farmers have been registered and 73,472 applications have been received so far. “Of these, 18,046 applications are under process, while 48,348 have been approved. A total of 9,131 units have been established,” the document reads. The document also mentioned the proposed introduction of a restructured Weather-Based Crop Insurance Scheme (RWBCIS) for fruit crops, including apple, saffron, litchi and mango. “The fresh tendering process for the scheme will be initiated after issuance of the revised RWBCIS operational guidelines by the Government of India,” the document reads.
